採用・広告の製品.quote: Qualitas builds AI-powered vision systems that automate visual inspection on your production line — catching defects the human eye misses, at full line speed, with measurable ROI in months.
Production lines deployed
Catch problems early and cut scrap, rework, and costly recalls.
Process & Video Analytics
Turns the cameras you already have into a continuous production and dispatch count — timestamped and reconciled against your ERP, with no new hardware on the floor.
Every Qualitas system runs the same proven three-stage vision pipeline — engineered end to end and tuned to your parts.
Our deep-learning models analyze each frame, locating and classifying defects with accuracy that improves over time.
Improvement in cost & efficiency
Functional Inspection of Precision Tweezers

A personal-care tool manufacturer needed repeatable functional checks of precision tweezers. Qualitas combined controlled part positioning, closing-force feedback and image analysis to evaluate how the tool functions, display the result and sort accepted and rejected parts.
Checking Biscuit Pack Contents and Carton Closure

Biscuit packaging needs more than a check of the finished box. Before cartoning, the line must verify the number and identity of the wrapped packs being loaded. After cartoning, it must inspect the carton closure and check the printed date and batch information.

Qualitas brought these tasks together through vision inspection at infeed and outfeed. The application covers two cartoning lines, with four vision systems and recipes for nine product variants. It combines product recognition, counting, carton inspection, character reading and communication with the line controls.

APIT and Qualitas co-developed the Total Mill Analyser, combining rice-industry machine-building expertise with machine vision and Intel technical collaboration. One unit has been delivered, and the product is being launched into the market.
Automated reading of cylinder tare weight and pressure-test due codes for HT Process Controls and IndianOil filling operations. Overdue cylinders are rejected from filling, across 150 deployments.
Six-Lane Cone Presence and Fragment Inspection

An ice-cream manufacturer needed to check cone and sleeve presence across six parallel positions. Qualitas delivered a camera-and-lighting system with EagleEye Edge analysis, PLC results and inspection history. The agreed damage check focused on loose cone pieces inside the cone.

An overhead camera and custom dome lighting let a pharmaceutical manufacturer count trays of vials at the loading station. EagleEye displays the detected count for product reconciliation before dispatch.
Camera, lighting, image capture and server transfer for an integrated steel manufacturer in India. Clear surface images from a red-hot production line, ready for the customer’s downstream analysis.
A cylinder-surface inspection pilot addressed the limited coverage of manual checks beside a conveyor. This project is separate from tare-weight reading and pressure-test validation.
3D vision inspection uses height and profile information to evaluate soldered electronic components. The inspection task concerns solder and pin conditions that require rejection.
Camera-based dimensional inspection checks defined features on engine housings. Stable part presentation and measurement references make the images useful for dimensional analysis.

For a brewery bottling line, Qualitas combined two triggered camera views with controlled lighting to check label presence, orientation, the selected label variant and rear batch-code presence. Pass/fail outputs connect the inspection to the line controls.
This page covers recognition of printed price and batch information on FMCG labels. The inspection image illustrates locating and checking the variable text.

Qualitas supplied the vision guidance for a robotic cell delivered through an automation integrator to an appliance manufacturer. The system located components and provided positions for robot pick and place.

A tabletop station for an anonymous tobacco laboratory reads a manufacturing date and laser-printed 14-digit packet code, captures the side-face barcode and writes the consolidated data directly into LIMS.
A moving cart provided an image-acquisition approach for the inner surfaces of large wind-turbine blades. The task was to capture useful views over an extended surface.

One line-scan camera and a line light image the deck of an engine block as it moves past, producing a 245-megapixel image. A checkerboard calibration tile ties the image to millimetres, for measurements with 30 µm accuracy.

AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRIES
The partnership extends beyond an inspection application for one factory. APIT and Qualitas have co-developed a product that is being brought to the rice-industry market.

A rotary inspection cell combines automated pre-shift calibration, top and side measurements, marking and sorting. Each spark-plug variant is supported through the appropriate inspection recipe and tooling. Operators load and unload the plugs manually; the machine moves each plug through the inspection positions and connects the camera decisions to the handling controls.

This makes the reference check part of the machine’s shift-start routine. Operators can establish that the inspection setup is measuring a known part correctly before relying on its decisions for production parts.

Maintenance controls provide manual indexing, camera triggering and movement of the handling mechanisms. Keeping these setup actions separate from normal production helps operators change variants while retaining a defined inspection sequence.

Qualitas developed an inline vision system for a global bearing manufacturer to inspect tapered rollers' curved surfaces and larger end faces. Three camera views, controlled red illumination and a trained inspection model identify the agreed surface conditions. The result appears on an operator display and is communicated to the line controller for rejection.

Image acquisition was a central part of the solution. The installation used three industrial cameras: two views of the curved surface and one of the larger end face. Controlled red illumination helped produce contrast on the reflective finish, while guides presented the rollers along a defined path.

The delivered system combined acquisition, software evaluation and automated rejection. Operators could see the result at the station, while the controller received the signal needed to act on the inspected component.

The practical value was a defined inline check of the agreed surfaces, with the inspection decision connected to physical segregation. It provided a basis for finding recurring manufacturing problems earlier and reduced reliance on visual sampling for these checks.

A plug that sits differently in its holder can produce a different apparent measurement even when the part itself has not changed. The application therefore combines a workpiece carrier with orientation and seating checks before the measurement sequence.

A part-presence sensor confirms that a plug is loaded. An orientation camera checks its presentation, while the loading position includes a safety light curtain. The rotary table then carries the plug through the top and side inspection positions. This gives the cameras a controlled view of the features rather than relying on an operator to hold each part in front of a camera.

This makes the reference check part of the machine’s shift-start routine. Operators can establish that the inspection setup is measuring a known part correctly before relying on its decisions for production parts.

Changeover involves both a software recipe and the matching physical carrier. The operator selects the variant on the display, verifies the selected name and uses the corresponding workpiece carrier and hex-head fixture. The setup also includes the appropriate top and side camera positions.
Image acquisition, trained surface inspection, an operator display and line-control integration connect selected-surface checks to physical rejection.

Image acquisition was a central part of the solution. The installation used three industrial cameras: two views of the curved surface and one of the larger end face. Controlled red illumination helped produce contrast on the reflective finish, while guides presented the rollers along a defined path.

The setup had to accommodate different roller sizes without relying on a new camera arrangement for every part. Positioning, focus and lighting therefore had to be considered together. A model can only judge what appears in its images: surface visibility and repeatable presentation were as important as the inspection software.
The camera arrangement viewed selected portions of the working surfaces. It should not be described as a full 360-degree surface scan.
The conveyor and guides carry the component through the imaging station.

The delivered system combined acquisition, software evaluation and automated rejection. Operators could see the result at the station, while the controller received the signal needed to act on the inspected component.

One camera looks into each cone position. Triggered lighting gives the software a consistent view of the wafer and sleeve, while the six positions are checked in the same inspection cycle. The camera arrangement follows the parallel lanes of the line.

Two line-scan cameras on a common axis image the row as a motor-driven tray carries it under a line light. Calibration software guides the operator through each set-up step, stitches the two views and measures every pellet.

Pellets sit in rows on a tray that a motor drives under the cameras. Each line-scan camera builds its image one line at a time as the row moves, and each covers part of the row. Together they cover the full length of about 400 mm.
